utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Douglas Stringer with Lisa Biersay, Thomas Laugel, and intern Marija Bukovac for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic, Christopher Gosnell, and our intern, Mr. James Foster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. A short oral ruling. The Trial Chamber is seized of the Prosecution notice concerning Exhibit P1513 and hereby grants the request to replace the exhibit. The Registry shall take any necessary action to implement this decision. Thank you. Next witness is ready, Ms. Biersay?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I believe so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, could I just ask if anyone's having any difficulties getting into e-court or is it just me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Do you need assistance? Is it okay now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, it's slow but it's now working. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: With the answer you gave me, I take it you can understand me -- you can hear me in a language you understand, traditional question. Could you please tell us your name and your date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Petr Kypr and I was born at the 8th of May, 1948.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And do you want to testify in English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am from Prague. I am Czech citizen and originally I am Czech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You are about to read the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I must point out to you that by doing so you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury should you give untruthful information to the Tribunal. Could you now read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Ms. Biersay, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Good morning. Are you comfortably seated where you are?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber what your current profession is.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I'm a diplomat. I am leader of analytical group and deputy head of policy planning department of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Czech Republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what rank do you hold?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: My diplomatic rank is ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Ambassador Kypr, I'd like to direct your attention to the period of September to December of 1991. Where were you working at that time?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: At that time I was posted by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs as the head of Czech delegation to the EC monitoring mission, and being for short time in Zagreb, then I had been as a deputy head of regional centre of EC monitoring mission to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And for the record could you tell us the meaning of EC, you say EC monitoring mission.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: EC monitoring mission was a body which has been established since very beginning of Yugoslav conflict, maybe to prevent the conflict. All the legislation you can see in the Memorandum of Understanding between Croatia, Serbia, and ECMM. ECMM in that time had been represented by monitors from 12 countries, and because it was not enough, they asked some other countries for support and one of these countries had been Czechoslovakia in that time and as well, for instance, Canada, as my colleague Cunningham was from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What was Cunningham's position with the ECMM? And before you answer that, does EC mean European Community?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, EC is European Community, afterwards the name has been changed to European Union.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, back to Mr. Cunningham, what was his position within the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I don't know his previous position, but in the regional centre Belgrade he had been the head of monitors.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Is that referred to in short form as HOM?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: HOM of regional centre Belgrade was Ambassador Michel Perrin, the French ambassador, but the whole operational issue was controlled by Hugh Cunningham as head of the monitors.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And head of monitors, is that shortened to HOM in some of the documents that --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it is the abbreviation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You touched a little bit upon the purpose for the creation of the ECMM. Could you describe to the Trial Chamber what was the mandate of the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Mandate of ECMM was rather limited. Our main task was to monitor cease-fire or if not exist at least the situation and to help to prevent bloodshed, to bring messages from one side to the other side to help them to communicate each other and these supportive things like to follow if there is -- there was some delegation coming from one side to the other side. So we were in the convoy only to monitor the situation and to confirm at least some safety of this delegation on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What was your specific role?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: My role in this mission was double. Once -- on one side I was a monitor, on the other side, because I knew local languages and I could speak fluently and I know the background even, so I was used for interpreting in cases when it has been necessary, for instance, when we didn't want to have an official interpreter from one or from the other side because usually teams of ECMM were equipped by some interpreter from JNA side, for instance. It was usually even liaison officer from JNA who was interpreting, but in certain cases it was, let's say, more independent or more safe for local people to speak directly to me than through interpreter. So then I was interpreting as well. On the other hand, I had to as a deputy head of mission work on preparations of tasks, more or less knowing the background of the situation from the press because I was following local media of both sides and trying to help the -- in the preparedness to the situation which can appear.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Have you testified before this Tribunal previously?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, I have been a witness in two cases, the last one was with -- was the case with Colonel Mrksic and Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And there was a third accused in that case as well.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, I know, but I don't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: No, it's okay. You testified for four days during that case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You were cross-examined by three Defence attorneys; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to direct your attention -- excuse me one minute. You were involved with evacuations from Ilok, is that correct, in October of 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And that was done pursuant to an agreement that was reached; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What was your participation in that evacuation?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: In the -- it started or our contacts with Ilok started, I don't remember exact date, but we got the message from Zagreb that there are some problems in this pocket which have been surrounded by the JNA. "Pocket" means few villages surrounding Ilok plus Ilok. So we went there with one team to see the situation. Then we were told that people are so scared that they are preparing referendum, if to stay and if to -- or to go west and if to give up weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Did you say "give up weapons"?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Hand-over weapons to JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, you testified about this in the Mrksic case so I won't go into extreme detail about this. What I'd like to do is to direct your attention to the morning of the evacuation. Could you describe to the Trial Chamber what you observed regarding the evacuees that morning in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: It was very sad moment because I slept in the neighbourhood. We didn't want to go to Belgrade, we wished to stay nearby to show that we are covering the situation and to make people more safe and not raise tensions. And so in the very morning the queue of these vehicles and people was built, and it was a very sad moment because I went around the whole queue and I saw how people were silently crying and there was plenty of cars and tractors I have never seen because they wished to move with whatever do they want, whatever do they have. So it was very, very quiet but very depressive moment, but I didn't took part in the evacuation because I had another task. So the other team came from Belgrade to follow the evacuation and I went to Belgrade for another task. So I have no idea what has happened afterwards, but the evacuation was as I was told without many problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to direct your attention to Lovas very briefly. You previously testified in the Mrksic case regarding Lovas; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Why did you go to Lovas?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: We got a message from -- "we" means EC monitoring mission regional centre Belgrade. We got a message from EC monitoring mission Zagreb that there are some problems in these villages especially in Lovas. So we asked for permission to go there. Usually we were supported from the JNA having the liaison officer, but in this case we are told that there are some irregulars from the Croatian side and that JNA cannot guarantee our safety. But because of urgency of this message we got, we decided to go anyhow there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Ambassador Kypr, if I could interrupt for one moment. Where were you when you got the message about the problems in Lovas?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I am not quite sure. It could be in Zagreb but even by mobile phone to the car in Ilok directly, but I believe that it has been in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when you say that "we were told that there were some irregulars," who told you that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And the liaison officer with which entity?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Means JNA, but I don't remember whom of them because they were in daily contact with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So you don't remember the specific person but you know it was the JNA?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you went to Lovas, did you, in fact, find irregulars from the Croatian side, as you had been told?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: No. We haven't found them, we haven't met them. What -- whom we met there were two groups of volunteers, Serb volunteers, one group on the road somewhere, the other group at the entrance to Lovas.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, in your testimony and in some of the exhibits, one in particular, you describe that visit so I won't cover that presently.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What I'd like to do now is ask perhaps that the binder -- and this is a binder that has been approved by the Defence and it contains some materials that will be relevant to Ambassador Kypr's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Ambassador Kypr, in your Mrksic testimony you discussed events and documents related to the ECMM's participation in evacuations from the Vukovar area in November of 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: One of those documents that you discussed, if we could now turn to tab 27, it's 65 ter number 5125. And, Ambassador Kypr, we won't go into detail for this document because it's previously discussed in your testimony, but what I -- in that document there are discussions about various evacuations in the area of Vukovar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It's the full coverage which has been done afterwards, I believe, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And, Ambassador Kypr, would you be comfortable drawing an illustrative map, very rough, just to indicate the various evacuations that were going on in the area?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could Ambassador Kypr be assisted in just drawing on a blank sheet of paper which I can provide and perhaps we can put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. From Vukovar there is --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: -- Danube river --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you put a V, perhaps, at the spot where you just called Vukovar --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes. This is Vukovar. There is the Danube river. There is Ilok. There are some villages, Bapska, Sarengrad, Mohovo. There is the village Lovas, approximately, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you describe -- let's start with the evacuations in which you participated in. Where did your -- where did those convoys travel from and to?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Okay. There were several convoys. Speaking about convoy from Vukovar's hospital, it means convoy with wounded and sick people which we were responsible to monitor. There were two convoys. First convoy went in the first day and it should go directly to the point of contact in Bosnia and further to Croatia, but because of some shooting on the way we were told then later on that it is not possible. So convoy went to -- from the hospital, so it will be first convoy of wounded people. It went to Negoslavci, then we were stopped and we got an information that it is not possible to go further to Bosnia and then to Croatia. So we went to Sremska Mitrovica, it is somewhere down, it is not in good form here, but I believe that for understanding it's -- of the Court it's enough. So this is Sremska Mitrovica and the first part of convoy was there overnight in -- there is a garrison with a hospital and we were received in this military hospital and wounded people were taken very seriously and with a lot of help. During the convoy, as I do remember, one lady and her baby died because of previous injuries or disease, I don't know. And one man was in such a difficult condition that we have to let him be here in this hospital and then he has been moved to Belgrade, I believe, but it was confirmed by my colleague Dr. Schou from EC monitoring mission, yes, that his health situation is such that he cannot be -- he cannot be -- he cannot travel to Croatia so --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Ambassador Kypr --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: -- this was the only case --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Excuse me --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: So this is the first --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Ambassador Kypr, one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you spell the name of your colleague, Schou?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: S-c-h-o-u, he is Danish.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay. So -- this -- and you were with this convoy; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, I have been with this convoy. Then overnight in Sremska Mitrovica, other team from Belgrade came to -- and we hand over the convoy to them, the first convoy, and then they followed to the contact for the hand-over to Croatian side so it was somewhere Brcko, I don't remember exactly the place. And we went back from Sremska Mitrovica - "we" means Dr. Schou and me - we went back for another convoy of wounded people and then we went directly to the place of the contact. So it is the second day.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you say "the first day," do you mean the 20th of November?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: So the one W that you have there for the first convoy with the wounded, that was the 20th?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: This is the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And the next one that you've now marked as 2W, that was the next day?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And that convoy you were also with; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And regarding -- if you could briefly just sketch the starting point and the end point of the other convoys that were assisted by your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: There were some more convoys for refugees. The main convoy went from Marinci, this is near Vukovar somewhere here, I believe, Marinci, and this convoy went on the 20th. But I don't know it personally but only from reports and from what I have been told by my colleagues there. So the 20th they started but they have to overnight -- to stay overnight somewhere on the road. I believe that it has been in Sremska Mitrovica but I don't know. So the next convoy went somewhere, it was the first refugee, let's say. And then the next day, they crossed borders from Serbia to Bosnia and then to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Where you placed an X, is that meant to be Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, the point of hand-over was mentioned -- was meant in Bosnia, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And could you put "Bosnia" underneath that X just so that it's clear.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And I think at this point the references to Lovas and Ilok are no longer relevant, so could you simply just make a line -- draw a line through that.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Okay. So it was this pocket and I believe that now it's obvious.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Okay. And does that complete the list of the evacuations that you're aware of from the Vukovar area in the November period?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: As I know, yes, at least what we have covered. But there were so many teams and we were so busy that really I have no complete memory about that because it was so exhausting to do only this convoy from Vukovar that I, frankly, have no time and neither interest to follow these things.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time we tender the illustration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit Number P1644. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador Kypr, that terminates our use of the ELMO. Ambassador Kypr, in your testimony you described the agreement that was reached between the JNA, the Croatian government to facilitate the evacuation from the Vukovar hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And in this regard, turning now to tab 4, which is 65 ter number 604, now I won't ask you many questions about this because it has been discussed previously in your testimony. By what name do you refer to this agreement?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: It was usually named as Raseta's Agreement during our negotiations, so this is the name I do remember during our negotiation with JNA about the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And why was it known as the Raseta Agreement?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Because for the Yugoslav People's Army it was signed by General Raseta who was the - how to say? - the main liaison or main representative of Yugoslav People's Army in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, the -- in the first paragraph, if we could blow that up, and again we won't be going into detail but I just wanted to indicate that the first paragraph describes the parties to the agreement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Are you able to see? I know that you've had eye surgery so if at any time it becomes difficult, please let me know.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And that paragraph describes the parties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And was ECMM a party to this agreement described in paragraph 1?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: No, the ECMM isn't mentioned in para 1, but it doesn't mean that we were not involved because there was valid this Memorandum of Understanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And directing your attention to paragraph 7, does that address the role of ECMM?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, we are mentioned there and it is -- it covers our task.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Directing your attention to paragraph 5, in your Mrksic testimony you described that this agreement did not allow the JNA to remove wounded prisoners of war from the Vukovar Hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what was ECMM's understanding of the scope of that paragraph? Who was it meant to cover?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: It has to cover all those wounded or sick people undergoing medical treatment in Vukovar's hospital. So it means that there were in Vukovar Hospital -- there were wounded Serbs, Croats, maybe some other nationalities because it was an open city before so I don't know. But definitely who I know is Serbian and Croatian people were there as wounded, as sick; Serb and Croat personnel as well in the hospital. So it was a very mixed society, civilians, military, so all these people were covered as we do understood this by this agreement, by the Article 5.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now directing your attention to, as you describe in your Mrksic testimony, the 19th of November where there were meetings held with the JNA right before the evacuation from the hospital on the 20th. During the November 19 meetings with the JNA, what was their view of the coverage for paragraph 5 of the Raseta Agreement? Was it consistent with the view of ECMM?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: No, it was not consistent neither with ECMM but what was the most important, it was not consistent with the agreement. First we were told that prisoners of war will be removed from the hospital and that they will be exchanged in appropriate time afterwards. And the second which appeared to be even bigger problem, it has been that we were told that there are Serb irregulars very angry with their losses in Vukovar or in Vukovar battle and that JNA cannot guarantee if there is a single Croatian soldier in the convoy, that they cannot guarantee the safety of convoy. And "they" means irregulars will attack the convoy, they will kill Croatian patients, whoever, JNA guard and as well as EC monitoring mission because they are very angry and very excited.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What was the reaction of the ECMM to this?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Colonel Cunningham, as very strong military -- strongly opposed that, saying, "Look, there is Article 5 and there are some rules for behaviour on the front line, Geneva Conventions, so you have to obey these things which were already signed and which are valid." The same behaviour was -- or the same position was taken by Dr. Schou.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What went through your mind when you heard that the JNA planned on removing wounded POWs from the convoy -- well, excluding them, I should say?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I was very scared because if JNA, which is superior on this territory, is saying that somebody else will do something and giving him this power, it means that they are giving him even some responsibility. So it -- for me it was very strange and I was really scared and -- but there was nothing to do then, only to make aware our partners that there is the Raseta Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move from the agreement to the actual evacuation itself. So I'd now like to move to the morning of the 20th of November, 1991. You and your team made your way towards the Vukovar Hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when you and your team arrived in the Vukovar centre, did you go immediately to the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: No. We were stopped -- the whole convoy was stopped before the bridge --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: One moment and excuse me, Ambassador Kypr. When you say "the whole convoy," at that time what was the convoy composed of?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: It was already prepared convoy for the evacuation. So there were -- in the beginning there were some military vehicles with people from local staff, let's say, some colonels and so on, so two, three vehicles then. Then some other military vehicle and then our car as EC monitoring mission. And behind us there were these buses, trucks, and military ambulances for the evacuation of wounded people.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: There were no evacuees yet --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: No, no, no, we were -- everything was prepared for evacuation and we were stopped before the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And for how long were you stopped before the bridge?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: It has been as a minimum one hour and a half, but I believe that it was two hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And whose decision was it to stop the convoy in the place it was stopped?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: It was some of the superior military. I don't remember if it has been Major Sljivancanin or somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And what was the reason given to you for stopping before the bridge for approximately two hours?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Demining, demining of the area because it's -- then it is dangerous for us to go through. So we have to wait until demining will be finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And who told you that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Military.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: JNA?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: From -- were you able to observe any demining activities from where you were?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: No, from the place we were stopped, there was not visible almost anything because in front of us there were military vehicles and the road is -- there is a curve. So it was not visible more and we can't see anything because there were -- on one side there was a huge building destroyed, some bodies were smelling there probably from this huge building. On the other side there was Danube and the Hotel Danube. So we were in such a place that there was not possible to see almost anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you finally were able to move towards the Vukovar Hospital and -- could you describe the situation outside of the hospital, what did you see? What did you smell?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: At the entrance of the hospital there were some five, maybe more, sanitary wagons, ambulances destroyed by shells. On the left side of the hospital there was standing a group of some 50 people, silent. Some of them were in white clothes, in white like doctors or medicine sisters. Then we went down to the cellar where the hospital has been for these three months existing. The situation outside of the hospital was very sad, especially this part of the city. I do remember that because I was travelling many times to the seacoast in peaceful time and it was really flourishing place and one of the richest places in this area, and then there were no one single tree without cut branches and one single roof untouched. The whole road was usually two tracks plus some grass plus "trottoirs," so it was relatively wide and the whole street was full of debris and destroyed cars. Only one way for one car was there opened. So it was really a sad, sad view. Then comparing to that, coming to hospital I was surprised because as these conditions were like this, that they were for a few months without water and electricity, they were lighting with batteries from cars used as the source of electricity. So it was in relatively good order and clean as much as possible. In that time it was Colonel Cunningham with us as Dr. Schou and me, so Colonel Cunningham visited the whole place. I went with him up to the roof to see the situation there. Hospital was without military presence from any side, so it was according the agreement. And then --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Ambassador -- excuse me, Ambassador Kypr, I wanted to just stop you there for a moment to ask you about your Mrksic testimony where you describe that after arriving at the hospital, the ECMM was informed that some people had been taken out of the hospital before you got there. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Could you describe to the Trial Chamber what the ECMM's reaction was to that information?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: This information -- Colonel Cunningham got this information from me because I was -- I was told it by somebody in the hospital, but I believe that he got the same message from the other side as well. It doesn't matter. So Colonel Cunningham was aware about this situation and because there was no communication at all in the down-town of Vukovar. So then he went to -- went back to Belgrade to settle the situation. Definitively we mentioned and we asked namely on Dr. Bosanac because we have been in a contact with her before by phone and she was known and she was a person of -- which could be in danger because of presentation of her in Serb press.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when you say the "presentation of her in the Serb press," what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: She was presented like Dr. Mengele.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You describe the details of the evacuation in your Mrksic testimony and so at this time I'd like to move from Vukovar and go to another topic. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: You described during your Mrksic testimony going to Lovas and you also described receiving information about maltreatment of -- well, you called the -- the difficult situation in Lovas and that you acted upon it. In your notebook which was admitted in the Mrksic case and in this case it's tab 34 which is 65 ter number 5673. And if we could go to page 25 of that. Now, regarding --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: No, no, no. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you have it?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, I have the page, 25.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Now, what is -- now, in addition to hearing about the difficult situation in Lovas, you also received information about the difficult situation in Berak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it is. But it has been two months later.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Correct. And the date of that is indicated in your notebook; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And is that 13th of December?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I don't remember that, but if it is written here it's the right date.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What information did you receive about the situation of Croats in Berak?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: There was -- as I do remember, the first information was not quite precise so it was only a signal that something wrong is going on in the village Berak.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: When you arrive -- did you go there?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: We asked for permission of JNA and, yes, we went there with our liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when you went there, what happened?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: We were received by the local staff of JNA because probably there was some unit situated. And then we have met with local mayor, I believe. We were told that situation there is calm, that there are no problems now at all, that there were some small clashes before, but then -- but now the situation is quite normal. To confirm that, I was brought to three houses of Croatian families because the village is on the Serb -- was on the Serb territory, and I was brought to three Croatian families and their owners confirmed that, yes, everything is okay. What has scared me that their wives were standing in the corner and were very sad or some of them were crying. So it repeated three times in these three houses, and then I got the message that in some farm of this village, in some house, big house of this village, that there are some detainees. So we went to this home. There was some 50 people at the age from 55 to over 80, I believe 85 or 88 was the eldest or oldest lady.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: What was the predominant gender of the detainees?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Over 60.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And were they men? Women?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: There were more women than men, I believe 1:2 or 1:3.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And when you say 1:3, is that a ratio?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Ratio.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Of men to women?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Men to women.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And did you have a chance to talk to these people?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, I spoke to them. We were told that they were told that they are isolated in this house because they were supportive or they could be supportive to their -- to members of their families who committed some attacks to -- against Serbs from these villages -- from this village.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And did they tell you whether or not they had done that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: No, they denied that and they were -- in reality they didn't know what is happening because they were not accused. They were not in contact with police, neither with -- there was no any medical care. The oldest lady was only laying in the bed in the house, what -- and probably it was not only -- only is alive there because they have to go to bring some food from what was the rest in their houses. So with guard they were -- they went for some food. And a colleague of mine who was there has shown me some bullets in the roof of the room they were sleeping. So it means that probably it was not -- it was not the battle because the bullets are usually in this level, horizontal level, not vertical one, so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'd like to now turn to page 28 of that document. There is a reference, it's the second block from the bottom of the page. It says: "Investigation, jail, and court." And it says: "Dalj SBWS." Do you recall what that was in reference to?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: This is because after meeting with these people, we were speaking with this local representation and we were told that they are isolated because of two reasons. One reason is to make them safer against the aggressivity of people who were touched by this -- these attacks of the Croatian terrorists and -- from their families, from the families of detainees. And the second reason was to prevent them not to supply these people, these terrorists, who are supposingly in the neighbourhood, in forests. So this what we have been told. There was a description of this explosion and who had some rifle. I don't remember details, but I was told that it was investigated by the police and that it had been before a court and we have to check it in the jail in Dalj which is the local centre of -- region -- of local region. And what is the abbreviation SBWS, I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to those 50 detainees in Berak?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I don't remember because I went to Zagreb afterwards so I didn't follow the situation there, but I believe because we got a real promise from the side of JNA that it will be settled from the side of our liaison officer. So I believe that it has been settled.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Ambassador Kypr, were you sent English audio files for your testimony in the Mrksic case?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yeah. I went through them. I listened to them all.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And did the audios correctly reflect the testimony that you gave over those four days?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And was your testimony in that case truthful?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And during that testimony you discussed many documents - we've only touched upon quite a few today; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: If you were asked the same questions today, would your answers be in substance the same?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. Only my memory is now a little bit weaker so I will rely more on papers than seven years ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time we tender tabs 36, 37, 38, and 39, which are the transcripts from the Mrksic case, and they are 65 ter numbers 5816, 5817, 5818, and 5819. We would also tender the associated exhibits listed in tabs 1 through 35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked. The Registrar will circulate a memo with the exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And thank you, Mr. Kypr.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: At this time I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Ambassador. Do I understand that the pronunciation of your last name is Kypr?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is that the correct pronunciation?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you. My name is Christopher Gosnell, Ambassador Kypr, and I am representing Mr. Hadzic in these proceedings. I have a few questions for you. If any of my questions are unclear, please feel free to ask for an elaboration or a clarification and I'll do my best. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, am I correct that in the reports that you prepared and in the keeping of your notebook that you did your best to be as full and complete as possible in identifying the participants in the events that you were observing?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Frankly not. The problem is that I was following the substance. The official names and situations were usually described or make notes by these people who were in the team and who were listening only one version, so translated version. So usually the remarks of Colonel Cunningham are better than mine because I was not following these formal things. I was more behind this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, would you agree with me, then, in the course of your documentation you do mention a great many names of the participants of the speakers --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Of course, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- of the people providing you with information. And the question that I asked you was whether you did your best to record those individuals who were providing that information?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I did my best in those circumstances because sometimes are people coming and the discussion was such that I cannot take care about these people. Sometimes I had a time to ask somebody to tell me who is -- who is coming. On the other hand, I didn't care if somebody went out even from the list. So I cannot guarantee that these people were sitting there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I understand you can't guarantee and I think you've answered my question which is I believe that you did do your best; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have Prosecution tab 11, which is 65 ter 5050.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, the document coming up on the screen in front of you is one of the exhibits associated with your testimony in the Mrksic case and it's a report dated the 8th of October, 1991. I'm right, am I not, that you yourself did not personally take part in this -- in the mission described in this report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Excuse me, I just notice Ambassador Kypr looking very intently at the screen and I just wanted to say that he does have the binder of hard copies if that would be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I will try to read it if --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But, Ambassador Kypr, just to make it easier, the binder you have in front of you, sir, you could actually --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I don't think that it would be better. I have to go through the translation to B/C/S because it's readable -- it's legible for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, it's your choice. If it would be easier, you could turn up the hard copy in the binder in front of you.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: What I do remember, I was not a member of this team.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But it's correct that you did visit the villages of Sarengrad --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- Bapska --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry, Ambassador, if you can wait until I finish my question, it will facilitate the transcription of the recording and then perhaps observe a brief pause, otherwise our exchanges can't be recorded. Am I right that you did visit the villages of Sarengrad, Bapska, Mohovo, Lovas, and Opatovac on the 16th and the 19th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I cannot testify or guarantee that I have been there in that very day. I have been in these villages but I cannot say anything about the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what I'd like you to direct your attention to, please, is the notation that says: "1500: Meeting with JNA CDR at the Danube bridge ..." followed by a meeting with the authorities of Ilok. A visit of the village of Sarengrad, visit of the convent Ilok, and then again meeting with the JNA CDR, north of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, this is written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, first of all, do I understand that that is the bridge connecting Backa Palanka in Serbia with Ilok in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, this is the bridge over Danube, the only in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And can you recall whether there was a JNA check-point at that bridge?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: There was JNA on both sides of the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And as you passed through with your liaison, were you -- I should first ask you: Were you at all times accompanied by a JNA liaison officer when you travelled in this region?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I am not quite sure. I believe that sometimes we were without him in Ilok.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And can you tell us physically how that worked when you approached a JNA check-point, did your liaison officer facilitate your passage through these check-points?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it was -- it was standard procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in respect of this particular visit here and you made similar visits around this time-period, do I understand correctly that in order to follow this itinerary you would have to pass from JNA-held territory into territory held by Croatian forces and then back into territory held by the JNA in respect of Sarengrad; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And physically, how again did that work crossing the lines? Were you accompanied into the Croatian territory by the JNA liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I believe that at least once there must be some JNA because we were providing the monitoring of exhumation of some dead bodies who were removed in one of these villages because they were buried only temporary and they were moved to the cemetery in Ilok. So -- and in that very time, I am sure that there was JNA present in this convoy. So at least once I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, let's approach this very concretely. If you were moving at the bridge from Backa Palanka to Ilok and you wanted to go meet the authorities, the Croatian local authorities in Ilok, did you pass a conflict line, let's put it that way, between the JNA and Croat forces?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: No. There was no conflict line. It was - how to say it? - maybe open city in this sense. On the other hand, yes, there was certain front line because what we were told by the JNA - and we saw that - that there is another bridge with some mines around. So yes, the city was prepared for certain defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in respect of a visit to Sarengrad by way of Ilok, on that journey, a journey of that nature, would you have been accompanied the whole way by a JNA liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I don't believe it. I am not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, when you yourself went to Lovas and Bapska, casting your mind back to that trip, can you recall whether throughout the duration of your journey you were in the company of a JNA liaison officer?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to page 3 of this document, please. There are conclusions listed. And this, sir, as you may recall is the lead-up to the evacuation of Ilok. And under "Conclusions" it says: "Arrangement at high level should be made to arrange an evacuation as soon as possible! "A team should be sent in two to three days to assess again on the situation. The team should get in touch with the local authorities and with the JNA." Now, do I understand this notation to mean that on the Croatian side you're supposed to get in touch with the local authorities and on the Serb side you're supposed to get in touch with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it is true. I don't remember contact with some local Serb authorities in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And am I right in thinking that the reason why the ECMM was addressing the JNA as its interlocutor was because it was the JNA that was in control of the region?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: At least JNA was our partner, so we were told in Zagreb: Please, these are your liaison officers. We were not provided by the Serb side by anybody else except of JNA liaisons. So it was the only contact even to -- probably to civil authorities, through these officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 512.1, which is Defence tab 66.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember - as this document is coming up - ever hearing about an ultimatum issued by a JNA commander to the residents of Bapska?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: We were given this document by the local authorities in Ilok, and I believe that it was not my team but some other team.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Here's what it reads at items 1 to 2. "Since residents of your village of Bapska have been peaceful so far and have not caused any problems to JNA units, we assume that there will be no problems in the future either. We request the following from you: "1. By 1600 hours, collect all the weapons in the village and bring them to Vikjaca, where a JNA organ will be waiting for you. "2. If this is not done by this time, you can count on your village ceasing to exist on the geographical map." Now, do you remember whether there were any ultimatums of a similar nature made to other villages?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I don't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But you do remember hearing about this particular ultimatum; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I can't think more than we -- yes, we received this document and I was not the person who were given and who were, let's say, informed about the details of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: We would tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I am trying to locate our tab number, but it's already part of his 92 ter package. So if I could just have some time to find that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It's true that it does form part of another document, but there's no English translation associated with this page of the other document. Therefore, that being the case, I would like to tender this document separately.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I believe that's one of the items that we modified last week, but I'm happy to check. If we wish -- if the Court wishes to admit this, then that's fine; if the Court would like just to give me a few minutes to try to find the corresponding exhibit, I could do that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Shall we MFI it in the meantime?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: No objections to that, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The Registrar says that MFI it would cause a little technical problem --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Understandably. So I believe that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So let's wait a few minutes and give you the time to check it, Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And I believe in the meantime it could be -- that it is tab 12. Perhaps in the -- during the break we could confirm it and come back to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So we'll hear from the parties after the break about this. Thanks. Just one moment, Mr. Gosnell. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, were you able to read the name of the person who signed this ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's difficult to read it for me. I can't read it with my eyes. Some major, but who is the person I can't see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador Kypr, on the 12th of October, 1991 -- and this document is 05053, Prosecution tab 12, but I will not ask for it to be called up. But on the 12th of October, you wrote in a report: "We were supplied by both sides with a copy of an ultimatum by the JNA," and this is "made on 11 October 1991 to the people of Ilok. The ultimatum was under the authority of the JNA, and we were told by the Ilok community that the officer in charge of the military district was General Arandjelovic." And then annex A of your report contains that document. Now --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I'm -- excuse me. I wondered if the witness could be shown the cover of this document to see whether or not this is actually his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, sir, if you perhaps could turn in your binder to Prosecution tab 12, if there is such a --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And we might as well now bring it up on the screen, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: And conveniently, this is the same document containing the Bapska ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my tab 12 I have not such a document. What is there, there is a "sporazum," it means draft of agreement for evacuation of Ilok or something like that. Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, let's use the document on the screen in front of us, then.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yeah, this is the first page here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, did you author this?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: No, the writing is of somebody else. I am not quite sure who it is, but not mine definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And your name --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Probably Mr. Waters from UK.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And your name there up at the top, what does that indicate?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: It means the leader of the team in that time. We were changing in teams as leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you participated in the events that are described in this report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if we can turn over to page 2 and look at item 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "We were supplied by both sides with a copy of an ultimatum by the JNA made on 11 October ... to the people" --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "-- of Ilok. The ultimatum was made under the authority of the JNA, and we were told by the Ilok community that the officer in charge of the military district was General Arandjelovic. Copy of ultimatum at annex A." Well, let's see if there is a translation of annex A of this document. Could we go to the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: On the screen, sir. I think it may or may not be in your binder. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I have in my binder draft translation maybe of official -- but it is not named as "ultimatum." It names -- the name is "agreement," "sporazum."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Except, sir, that in your report or in this report, it is indeed described as an ultimatum; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, but it is described by the people from -- who were writing that, they -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, could we please have 05053, please, which is Prosecution -- I'm sorry, 05055, which is Prosecution tab 13. And if we could please go over to -- after we've looked at the front page for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is this document familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: It's not a document of my team, but generally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You've seen this document before and you know it to be an authentic ECMM document and report?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yeah. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 4. Perhaps we should start with page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, that document there on the right-hand side of the screen, is that the --

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, this is the same document we have mentioned as annex A before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And now I see it just disappeared.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And is that indeed the document that's referred to in the previous document which is described in the previous document as an ultimatum and here we see that it's headed as an agreement?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Even in previous report it was headed as the agreement. So I can't see the difference. Maybe there are some more remarks in --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, that wasn't my question and we needn't spend time on that. But let's just go, if we can, to point 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And perhaps we could just slightly move the English over so that we can see ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, I see the time. Would this be an appropriate moment or would you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could I just ask two or three questions and then we'll be done with this document or -- I'm in the Court's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: How long would you take? Depending on the answers?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I say probably it's prudent to take the break now then, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Ambassador, we will take the first break now. We will come back at 11.00. The court usher will escort you out of court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. President, I could use this time to take care of a couple of housekeeping matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The first being that there appears to be a slight omission in the transcript at page 28, lines 6 and 7. I believe that my question was whether or not that was the bridge connecting Backa Palanka, Serbia, with Ilok, Croatia. And the second point has to do with a document the Prosecution and I have been discussing over the break. I know the Prosecution is going to give their view in a moment. We do maintain the tendering of 65 ter 00512.1. Although it is very, very close to the document P316, there is a notation on that document by a witness and there is also a third page. And we would just like to have an unmarked version of this document without the third page. Even though it's identical, we just -- for our purposes, we think it's cleaner to admit the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just for completeness' sake, I would also like to add that the ultimatum is part of tab 11 on page 7, and it's an under seal document so we can't show it in public. So P316, as mentioned by the Defence, and tab 11, page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay, I take it when I look at your exhibit list that tab 11, which is 65 ter 5050 --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- is not P316?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Oh, no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: -- it's a different version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It's a different version?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And now the Defence asked for the admission of a third version?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Essential -- that's correct, Your Honour. And essentially it's -- they're asking for one page of 316, so a different version of one page of P316. But we have no objections. I was trying to be helpful and I may have caused more problems than helped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell, a different version of one page?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: P316 is a version of this document that was marked by a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And that also has a third page which indicates extraneous information. It is true that this document is a part of Prosecution tab 11. Nevertheless, we think it would be helpful to have this document separately. If we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Which is only one page of that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And why, if I understood you well, you're referring to 5051.1.2.1? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I haven't checked the numeration since the documents were exhibited, but that sounds correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is that -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So now the Registrar tells me that you tendered Exhibit Number 51 -- no -- well, 65 ter number -- no, exhibit number? 65 ter 512.1; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: That's right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Shall be assigned Exhibit Number D36. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, in front of us we have the -- this document which is the one that is either an ultimatum or an agreement. It's been described in the report as an ultimatum and here at the top we see that it's an agreement. Just focusing there on point 6 -- and this again, just to -- for the record, this is the alleged ultimatum/agreement of the 11th of October in respect of Ilok. Point 6: "JNA units shall take up positions in the town and set up the town's command ensuring peace until the situation stabilises." Now, again, just for the record, I apologise to have to interrupt my question, but this is a draft translation and we say a better translation of the words used is that: "The JNA units shall take possession of the town and set up the town's command ensuring peace until the situation stabilises." Now, my question, sir, is: Do you recall that, in fact, it was the JNA's intention during this time-period to take possession of the towns in this area?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Definitely it is said in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you ever hear Major-General Arandjelovic threaten to flatten Ilok to the ground if Croat forces did not surrender?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I don't remember that in these words. So I remember some threatening but not in these words. Because there were -- on the other side of the Danube there were tanks and it's 100 metres to the city, so they can do whatever they want. There were boats on Danube as well, military boats, so -- and from the other side there were as well present, mean JNA, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: As you've testified in the Mrksic case and now that testimony is before this Chamber, there ultimately was an agreement reached between the Croat side and the JNA in respect of the surrender of Ilok. And am I correct that your role was purely passive; in other words, to observe those negotiations and not participate in those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But you did observe them; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: We were there as monitors. We were asked by local authorities of city Ilok to be there to make a guarantee of their safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you were in the building where the negotiations were occurring; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, we were in the building with drivers and with other persons, but the negotiating teams were in another room.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you observed who entered that room; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I don't remember if I see some persons. So it is written on this agreement who made this agreement, but I cannot testify.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But Major-General Arandjelovic was there; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I don't remember, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: As far as you know, Goran Hadzic has no role whatsoever in these negotiations; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I don't remember, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you also not remember whether there was anyone at all from the regional Serbian government that had anything at all to do with these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I cannot say it because it was in a school and I am not quite sure if everybody was presented to us and named. So I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But you know, sir, that none of your documents indicate any presence at all by anyone from the Serbian district government?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it is so -- but, on the other hand, I cannot deny that so --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So I'm correct in saying that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 5077, which is Prosecution tab 20. And if we could please go over to page 2 of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, you say that you were only observers in respect of these negotiations, but is it true that Colonel Cunningham conveyed orders from the Croatian government in Zagreb to the local Croatian authorities in Ilok?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I don't think that it has been an order, but yes, there was some communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What was the content of that communication?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I don't remember precisely but it is mentioned in some of reports of Mr. Cunningham, so I believe that we can take it as a granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, let's go over to page 3 of this document. And this, sir, is a letter or some kind of a written communication by Ambassador Perrin who is, as I understand it, defending you and Colonel Cunningham against accusations by the Croatian government that you had improperly facilitated ethnic cleansing and even genocide in respect of Ilok. And Ambassador Perrin says - and if we can just turn over the page, please - and this is a quote: "Finally, when Cunningham relayed Zagreb's direct order to the village senior personnel to cease and desist in any activities that could be construed as aiding the evacuation, the spokesman for the villagers stated, quote, 'We are totally neutral. The presence of the mission is our only guarantee not to be killed -- I don't see and exit for us. We are victims. We can't have control. Army can do own work. And Ilok may not exist and Ilok will be same as Sarengrad and Bapska.'" Now, as far as you can recall, is that right that the order that Cunningham conveyed was that senior personnel should cease any involvement in the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I still can't see as an order because if it is an order, then there is no evacuation, if they are obeying these orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, the words used there are "direct order"; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, you want to characterise it as an instruction, I won't argue with you about that, but was it the case that this order or instruction was not only to cease engaging in the evacuation, but in fact to continue to fight the JNA?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I can't read it in these words, but maybe -- no, I can't read it. I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 05067, please, which is Prosecution tab 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Biersay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Thank you. It's just a reminder that this is an under seal document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now that I look at it, I see that's the case, so perhaps it could just not be displayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, if you -- looking at this document, is this a document that you prepared?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: No, it is written by somebody else. Only probably there are some remarks down on the page made by me, but I'm not quite sure. Yes, Colonel Grahovac at the bridge, it is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's turn over to page 2, please. And at point A: "Contact with Colonel Grahovac at 1100 at Ilok bridge," and again, just for the record, the date of this is the 19th of October, 1991, so this is after the evacuation of Ilok. "Contact with Colonel Grahovac at 1100 on Ilok bridge. From Colonel Grahovac: "Ilok and villages Sarengrad, Bapska, Mohovo, Lovas are safe and quiet and under JNA control. [As read] "The JNA is going at Sunday to establish a civilian municipal council. It's prohibited for the people of Ilok to get out of their home from 1800 to 1700 ..." Now, I want to specifically ask you about the JNA setting up a civilian municipal council. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. I don't remember even -- I was not there in that time, I believe, so I have no idea about the municipal council.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you remember whether there was a curfew in effect?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I don't remember, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And this document says that these other villages are safe and quiet and under JNA control, and then down at point 4 there's some more discussion about those other villages. And it says: "Situation in the other villages (Sarengrad, Bapska, Mohovo), as previous reports. "5. We didn't visit Lovas because darkness and problems with JNA controls. "6. Presence of plus -- or around 1 company JNA in the three villages west of Ilok." Now, we talked about this earlier, but am I correct in understanding that on the 19th of October, 1991, as far as you knew, there were JNA controls throughout this region?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yes, according this report they were controlling that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And were they controlling access to these villages?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I cannot say because I don't understand, I don't know, to which reports, report or reports, is referring to point 4 because there could be some reports I don't know or maybe some reports from our time, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I'm not so much interested in point 4, but rather point 5: "We didn't visit Lovas because darkness and problems with JNA controls." Can you answer this: Do you remember whether you had any delays when you were passing through these JNA controls in this area?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Sometimes yes, sometimes no. I do remember that we were waiting for two hours for some meeting which it should be in few minutes, and in the very moment we turn over and went back to Belgrade then they came. So there are different situation, and I was not there so I cannot explain it and probably my testimony in that will rely only on that I can confirm that this document is existing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, you were there on the 16th of October, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: I don't remember, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, one of your reports is dated the 16th of October and you say you went to Lovas.

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: Yeah, if it is written in the document, but I told you that I don't remember numbers. It's a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Never mind numbers, never mind dates. We know from one of your previous reports that you went to Lovas. On the occasion of that visit when you went to Lovas and I presume other villages, do you remember being controlled at JNA check-points on your way into those villages?

utterances.speaker: PETR KYPR
utterances.text: What I do remember that during this way we have already mentioned to Lovas when I have met with this local authority and was given by the list that people, I do remember that we were alone and I can confirm that because at the end of Ilok we had no coverage from JNA so I asked my driver: Please stay here in Ilok because it's not necessary to risk so much so we can drive the car ourselves, mean Cunningham and me. So I know that in that time there was no JNA. And at the end I was translating in Ilok and I do remember that this guy was insisting on some translation and I couldn't found appropriate English term. So I remember this, how he was insisting. So liaison officer was not there to help me. So I do know these things. There is nothing I can say more.
